tool.name: Jupyter
tool.tagline: Interactive notebooks for code, results and narrative in one document
tool.description: Jupyter is the open-source platform behind notebooks: documents that mix live code, its output (tables, charts, widgets) and Markdown text. JupyterLab and Jupyter Notebook are the browser interfaces, kernels run the code (Python via IPython, and dozens of other languages), and tools like nbconvert and papermill turn notebooks into reports and pipelines. It is the default workspace for data analysis, teaching and research.

glossary.def: In Jupyter, the separate background program that runs a notebook's code and remembers its variables. Each open notebook has its own kernel.
One box in a notebook: a code cell holds code you run, with its output shown underneath; a Markdown cell holds formatted text.
An improved interactive Python (a REPL with extras like better completion and magic commands). It is the kernel that runs Python code in Jupyter.
The number in brackets next to a notebook cell, like [5]: the order in which that cell was last run.
Variables and values in a notebook's kernel that the cells on screen no longer explain, because cells were run out of order, edited or deleted.
The main browser interface for Jupyter: a workspace with notebooks, files, terminals and panels. Jupyter Notebook is the simpler one-document-per-tab version.
The background program, started by jupyter lab, that serves the Jupyter pages to your browser, manages files and starts the kernels.
A standard way to write maths formulas as plain text, like $E = mc^2$ or \frac{a}{b}, which tools then display as proper formulas.
The two modes of a notebook. In edit mode keys type into a cell; in command mode (press Esc) keys act on whole cells, e.g. A inserts a cell above.
A searchable list of every action in an editor such as JupyterLab or VS Code, opened with a keyboard shortcut, showing each action's own shortcut.
The Python package that provides Jupyter's Python kernel. Installing it into an environment lets that environment run notebooks.
A small kernel.json file that tells Jupyter how to start one kernel: which program (e.g. which Python) to run and what name to show in the kernel menu.
A special IPython command starting with % (for one line) or %% (for a whole cell), like %timeit, that is not Python but is handled by the notebook's kernel.
An interactive control such as a slider, dropdown or button shown in a notebook and linked to a Python value in the kernel.
An add-on package that gives JupyterLab new features, such as a Git panel or better code completion.
Jupyter's tool for turning a notebook into another format, such as a web page (HTML), PDF or Python script, optionally running it first.
A tool that runs a notebook from the command line with chosen parameter values and saves the run, outputs included, as a new notebook.
A tool that keeps each notebook paired with a plain-text script version, so the script can be read, compared and reviewed like normal code.
A tool that removes outputs from notebooks automatically when you commit them to Git, keeping the history small and readable.
A tool that compares and merges notebooks cell by cell, instead of showing raw file differences.
A dict that maps format names (MIME types such as text/html or image/png) to the same output in each format, so the viewer can pick the best one it can show.
A label attached to a notebook output so that it can later be updated in place, for example a progress message.
The official structure of a .ipynb notebook file (a JSON layout of cells, outputs and metadata), and the Python library for reading, creating and checking such files.
The Python library that runs a notebook: it starts a kernel, sends it each code cell in turn and stores the outputs. nbconvert and papermill use it.
A messaging library that lets programs send each other messages over network connections with little code. Jupyter kernels talk to the outside world through it.
The set of JSON message types (execute_request, stream, status and so on) that Jupyter interfaces and kernels exchange to run code and return results.
A small JSON file written when a kernel starts, listing the address, port numbers and secret key that other programs need to talk to that kernel.
A Jupyter service for groups: it logs users in and starts a separate Jupyter server for each person, on one machine or across many.
Forwarding a port on your computer through an encrypted SSH connection to a port on a remote machine, so you can reach a service there that isn't exposed to the network.
The configuration library Jupyter uses: settings are attributes on named classes, like c.ServerApp.port = 9000, set in a config file or on the command line.

concepts.name: Notebooks, cells and execution order
concepts.summary: A notebook is a list of code and text cells run by a kernel; results depend on the order you ran cells, not where they sit.
concepts.why: Almost every notebook surprise, from 'NameError' to out-of-date results, comes from how cells and run order work.
concepts.body:
A script runs from top to bottom every time. A **notebook** lets you run a program one piece at a time and see each result right under the code that made it, mixed with your own notes. Jupyter is the most popular notebook tool; its files end in `.ipynb`.

A notebook is a list of **cells**. A code cell holds Python. Run it with Shift+Enter, and its output appears right below it and is saved in the file: printed text, the value of the last line, a chart or a table.

A Markdown cell holds formatted text: headings, lists, links and maths formulas. It is written in **Markdown**, a simple way to mark formatting in plain text, like `**bold**` or `# Heading`. So a notebook can read like a report.

Your code doesn't run inside the page. It runs in a separate background program called the **kernel**; for Python that is the **IPython** kernel, an improved version of the REPL. Like the REPL, the kernel remembers everything: a variable created in one cell can be used in any cell you run afterwards.

The number in brackets next to a cell, `[5]`, is its **execution count**: the order in which cells were run. That order, not the position on the page, decides what the kernel holds. You can run cell 7 and then cell 2, edit cell 2 and rerun it, or delete a cell whose variable the kernel still remembers. The result is **hidden state**: the notebook on screen no longer explains the results.

Habits that avoid trouble:

- Run cells top to bottom, and keep the notebook working in that order.
- Before sharing, use **Restart Kernel and Run All Cells**. If anything fails, the notebook was relying on hidden state.
- Keep cells small, one step each: load data, change it, chart it.

Only the last line of a cell is shown automatically, and only if it has a value (like `total` or `2 + 3`). Use `print()` or `display()` for anything else.
concepts.code:
# Cell [1]
prices = [3.5, 4.0, 2.25]

# Cell [2]
total = sum(prices)
total                      # last expression is displayed: 9.75

# Cell [3] - later edited to: prices = [1, 2] and re-run
prices = [1, 2]

# Cell [2] is NOT re-run automatically, so `total` is stale:
print(total)               # 9.75, although sum(prices) is now 3
print(sum(prices))         # 3
# Fix: Kernel > Restart Kernel and Run All Cells
takeaways: Cells share one kernel; the order you ran them decides its state
Only the value of a cell's last line is shown automatically
Restart and Run All before trusting or sharing results
pitfalls: Deleting a cell and assuming its variables are gone; the kernel keeps them until it restarts.

quiz.q: You ran cells in the order 1, 3, 2. What decides the values of variables now?
options: The order of cells on the page
The outputs saved in the file
quiz.explain: The kernel carries out code in the order you ran it; position on the page doesn't matter.

concepts.name: Installing and launching JupyterLab
concepts.summary: Install JupyterLab into a project environment, start it, and understand which programs run where.
concepts.why: Setting Jupyter up per project avoids the classic 'module not found in the notebook' confusion.
concepts.body:
Jupyter has two main apps for working with notebooks. Both open in your web **browser** (Chrome, Firefox, Safari) and both are run by the same background program, the **Jupyter Server**:

- **JupyterLab**: a full workspace with a file browser, tabs, notebooks side by side, terminals and add-ons.
- **Jupyter Notebook 7**: a simpler interface with one document per tab, built from JupyterLab's parts.

Install it into your project's **virtual environment**: a folder (here `.venv`) holding a private copy of Python plus the libraries this project uses. **pip**, Python's installer, puts libraries into it. Notebooks started from there see exactly the libraries your code sees:

```bash
python -m venv .venv               # create the environment
source .venv/bin/activate          # switch this terminal to it
pip install jupyterlab
jupyter lab
```

`jupyter lab` starts a small **web server** on your own computer: a program that answers your browser's requests. Its address is usually `http://localhost:8888`, where **localhost** means "this computer". Your browser opens it with a **token** in the address, a long random password that keeps other people out. The folder you start from becomes the top of the file browser. Stop everything with Ctrl+C in the terminal, or File > Shut Down.

Three programs are now running: the server, in your terminal; the browser page, which only shows things and sends your code across; and one kernel per open notebook, which actually runs the code. Closing the browser tab does not stop the kernels; use the Running panel to shut them down.

Editors understand notebooks too: VS Code, PyCharm and others open `.ipynb` files directly and start kernels without a separate server. Online services such as Google Colab run notebooks on their own computers. The files and kernels are the same everywhere.

`jupyter server list` shows the running servers and their addresses if you lose the tab.
concepts.code:
# Per-project setup
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate          # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install jupyterlab pandas

jupyter lab --version              # 4.6.x
jupyter lab                        # opens http://localhost:8888/lab?token=...
jupyter lab --no-browser --port 8890   # e.g. on a remote machine

# In another terminal
jupyter server list                # running servers with their token URLs
takeaways: JupyterLab and Notebook 7 are two interfaces on the same Jupyter Server
Install Jupyter in the project's virtual environment, then run `jupyter lab`
Server, browser page and kernels are separate; closing a tab leaves kernels running
pitfalls: Installing Jupyter outside the project environment and the libraries inside it, so imports fail in the notebook.

quiz.q: You close the browser tab of a running notebook. What happens to its kernel?
options: It keeps running until shut down or the server stops
It is converted to a script
quiz.explain: The browser page only shows the notebook; the kernel is a separate program the server started, and it must be shut down explicitly.

concepts.name: Markdown and rich output
concepts.summary: Write formatted Markdown cells with maths, and show tables, images, web content and charts from code.
concepts.why: Rich output is what turns a notebook into a readable analysis rather than a script full of print statements.
concepts.body: **Markdown cells** support headings (`#`, `##`), bold and italic, lists, links, images, code blocks, tables and maths formulas written in **LaTeX**, the standard text notation for formulas (`$E = mc^2$` inside a line, `$$...$$` on its own line). Press Shift+Enter to show the cell formatted, and double-click to edit it again. Headings also build JupyterLab's table of contents panel, which helps you move around long notebooks. **Code cells** show the value of their last line in the richest form that value offers. That is why a table from the pandas library appears as a neat grid and a chart appears as a picture. Such values can describe themselves in several forms, as **HTML** (the language web pages are written in), as an image, or as plain text, and JupyterLab picks the best one it can show. To show more than the last line, or to show results from inside loops and functions, use `display()`. It is available automatically in notebooks, or import it from `IPython.display`. That module also has helpers: - `Markdown("**bold**")` and `HTML("bold")` show formatted text that your code builds; - `Image("plot.png")` or `Image(url=...)`, `SVG`, `Video`, `Audio`; - `JSON(data)` for a fold-out tree view in JupyterLab. End a line with `;` to hide its value, for example after a charting call that returns objects you don't want printed. Outputs are saved in the notebook file. Big images and huge tables make the file large and make it hard to see what changed between two versions. So avoid printing whole huge tables: `df.head()` or `df.sample(5)` is usually enough.
concepts.code:
from IPython.display import display, Markdown, HTML
import pandas as pd                # a table library: pip install pandas

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Oslo", "Lima"], "temp": [4.5, 19.0]})

display(Markdown(f"**{len(df)} cities**, warmest: *{df.loc[df.temp.idxmax(), 'city']}*"))
display(df)                        # shown as a formatted table
html = df.to_html(index=False)
display(HTML(html))

for city in df.city:
    display(Markdown(f"- {city}"))  # display works inside loops

df.temp.mean()                     # last line is shown: 11.75
# In a notebook, Markdown and HTML appear formatted; in the plain
# Python REPL you'd see their text version instead.
takeaways: Markdown cells give headings, lists, links and LaTeX maths
A cell's last value is shown in its richest form; `display()` shows anything else
`IPython.display` has Markdown, HTML, Image, JSON and media helpers
pitfalls: Displaying a whole million-row table or huge images, which bloats the saved notebook.

quiz.q: Inside a for loop you want each pass to show a table nicely formatted. What do you use?
options: Just write df on its own line
quiz.explain: Only a cell's last line is shown automatically; display() shows rich output from anywhere.

concepts.name: Command mode, edit mode and shortcuts
concepts.summary: Move between edit and command mode and use the core keyboard shortcuts to work quickly in notebooks.
concepts.why: A dozen shortcuts make notebook work several times faster than reaching for menus.
takeaways: Esc enters command mode, Enter enters edit mode
Shift+Enter runs and advances; A/B insert cells; D,D deletes; M/Y switch cell type
The command palette lists every action and shortcut
pitfalls: Typing while in command mode and accidentally deleting or converting cells; press Z to undo a deletion.

quiz.q: You are in command mode and press M. What happens?
options: The letter m is typed into the cell
The selected cell becomes a Markdown cell
The cell is merged with the next one
quiz.explain: In command mode M converts the selected cell to Markdown; Y converts it back to code.

concepts.name: Kernels and environments
concepts.summary: Understand what a kernel is, restart and interrupt it, and make virtual environments or other languages available as kernels.
concepts.why: Picking the wrong kernel is the number one cause of 'it works in the terminal but not in the notebook'.
concepts.body:
A kernel is the separate program that runs a notebook's code and holds its variables. The browser page sends it your code and shows the output it sends back. For Python the kernel comes from the **ipykernel** package, built on IPython. Kernels also exist for R, Julia, JavaScript, Rust, Go and many more languages.

Each kernel runs with one specific Python interpreter, and therefore one virtual environment with its own installed libraries. A **kernelspec**, a small `kernel.json` file, tells Jupyter how to start a kernel. To make a project's environment available in a Jupyter installed somewhere else:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pip install ipykernel
.venv/bin/python -m ipykernel install --user --name myproj --display-name "Python (myproj)"
```

Then pick "Python (myproj)" from the kernel selector. `jupyter kernelspec list` shows the registered kernels, and `jupyter kernelspec uninstall myproj` removes one. Inside a notebook, `import sys; sys.executable` tells you which Python is running it.

Kernel controls:

- **Interrupt** (I, I or the stop button) raises `KeyboardInterrupt` in the running cell, useful for a loop that never ends.
- **Restart** clears all variables and imports; use it after upgrading a library or when the state is confusing.
- If a kernel **dies**, all its state is lost and you must rerun the cells. The usual causes are running out of memory, or a crash inside a library written in C.

Install libraries from a notebook with `%pip install package`. That magic command always installs into the kernel's own environment. `!pip install` may instead run a different pip, whichever the terminal would find first, and install somewhere else.
concepts.code:
# Register a project environment as a kernel
python -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -q ipykernel
.venv/bin/python -m ipykernel install --user --name myproj \
    --display-name "Python (myproj)"

jupyter kernelspec list
#   myproj     /home/me/.local/share/jupyter/kernels/myproj
#   python3    /usr/local/share/jupyter/kernels/python3

cat ~/.local/share/jupyter/kernels/myproj/kernel.json
# {"argv": [".../.venv/bin/python", "-m", "ipykernel_launcher", "-f",
#   "{connection_file}"], "display_name": "Python (myproj)", "language": "python", ...}

jupyter kernelspec uninstall -y myproj
takeaways: A kernel is the program that runs your code; each uses one interpreter and environment
Register environments with `python -m ipykernel install --user --name ...`
Use `%pip install` in notebooks so libraries land in the kernel's environment
pitfalls: Running `!pip install` and installing into a different environment than the kernel uses.

quiz.q: A library imports fine in your terminal's venv but fails in the notebook. What should you check first?
options: Whether the notebook's kernel uses that venv's Python (sys.executable)
quiz.explain: The kernel decides which Python runs; if it belongs to a different environment, the library isn't installed there.

concepts.name: IPython magics and shell commands
concepts.summary: Use magic commands such as %timeit, %%time, %run, %pip and %autoreload, plus ! terminal commands, from a notebook.
concepts.why: Magic commands give timing, reloading and terminal access in one word each, and they appear constantly in notebooks you will read.
concepts.body:
The IPython kernel understands extra **magic commands** that are not Python:

- **Line magics** start with `%` and apply to the rest of the line.
- **Cell magics** start with `%%`, must be the first line of a cell, and apply to the whole cell.

The ones you will use most:

- `%timeit expr` runs a statement many times and reports the average time and how much it varied; `%%timeit` times a whole cell.
- `%%time` (or `%time`) measures a single run, both clock time and time the processor actually spent working.
- `%run script.py` runs a file inside the notebook, leaving its variables available.
- `%pip install pkg` installs into the kernel's environment.
- `%load_ext autoreload` then `%autoreload 2` re-imports your edited modules before each cell runs, essential when you edit a `.py` file alongside a notebook.
- `%matplotlib inline` or `%matplotlib widget` picks how charts are drawn: as fixed pictures, or as interactive ones.
- `%who` and `%whos` list your variables; `%env` reads or sets environment variables, named settings passed to programs.
- `%%writefile file.py` saves the cell to a file; `%%bash` runs the cell as terminal commands, and `%%html` shows it as a web page.
- `%debug` opens a step-by-step debugger at the last error; `%prun` reports which functions took the time.

Lines starting with **`!`** run terminal commands: `!ls data/` lists files. You can capture the output into Python, `files = !ls *.csv`, and put Python values into the command with braces: `!echo {name}`.

`%lsmagic` lists all magics and `%timeit?` shows help for one. Magics only work in IPython kernels, so a notebook full of them won't run as a plain `.py` script.
concepts.code:
%load_ext autoreload
%autoreload 2

nums = list(range(10_000))
%timeit sum(nums)          # e.g. 290 µs ± 50 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, ...)
%time total = sum(x * x for x in nums)
print(total)               # 333283335000

name = "jupyter"
!echo hello {name}         # hello jupyter
files = !ls /
print(type(files).__name__, "usr" in files)   # SList True

%env APP_MODE=dev
import os
print(os.environ["APP_MODE"])                  # dev
takeaways: `%` line magics apply to one line; `%%` cell magics to the whole cell
%timeit/%%time for timing, %run for scripts, %autoreload for live module edits
`!cmd` runs terminal commands; `x = !cmd` captures the output, `{var}` inserts Python values
pitfalls: Putting a `%%` cell magic anywhere but the first line of the cell, which raises an error.

quiz.q: You edit a function in mymodule.py, but the notebook keeps using the old version after re-running `import mymodule`. What fixes this from now on?
quiz.explain: Python imports a module only once and reuses it; autoreload re-imports changed modules before each cell runs.

concepts.name: Interactive widgets with ipywidgets
concepts.summary: Add sliders, dropdowns and buttons to notebooks with interact and ipywidgets, and react to changes with observe.
concepts.why: Widgets turn a notebook into a small app: move a slider and watch the results update, without editing code.
concepts.body:
The **ipywidgets** library gives you interactive controls, called widgets, shown right in the notebook. Each one is linked to a Python object in the kernel: move a slider and its value in Python changes too. Install it in the kernel's environment (`%pip install ipywidgets`); JupyterLab 4 and Notebook 7 support it with no extra steps.

The fastest route is `interact`, which builds controls from a function's parameters. Writing `@interact(...)` on the line above `def` hands the function to `interact`:

```python
from ipywidgets import interact
@interact(n=(1, 100), kind=["linear", "log"])
def show(n=10, kind="linear"): ...
```

A tuple becomes a slider, a list a dropdown, a bool a checkbox, a string a text box. The function reruns every time a value changes; `interact_manual` adds a Run button instead, for slow functions.

For more control, create widgets yourself: `widgets.IntSlider(min=0, max=10)`, `Dropdown`, `Text`, `Button`, `Checkbox`, `DatePicker`. Arrange them with the layout widgets `HBox` (side by side), `VBox` (stacked), `Tab` and `Accordion`. Each widget has a `value`. To react to changes, give the widget a function to call later, a **callback**:

- `w.observe(callback, names="value")`: the callback gets a dict holding the `old` and `new` values;
- `button.on_click(callback)`;
- `widgets.link((a, "value"), (b, "value"))` keeps two widgets in step.

Send printed text and charts from callbacks into a `widgets.Output()` area, by printing inside `with out:`; otherwise they may vanish.

Widgets need a running kernel; in a notebook exported as a web page they show their last state at best. For apps to share with others, look at Voila, Streamlit or Dash.
concepts.code:
import ipywidgets as widgets

price = widgets.FloatSlider(value=10, min=0, max=50, step=0.5, description="Price")
qty = widgets.IntSlider(value=3, min=1, max=20, description="Qty")
total = widgets.Label()
log = []

def update(change=None):
    total.value = f"Total: {price.value * qty.value:.2f}"

def remember(change):
    log.append((change["old"], change["new"]))

price.observe(update, names="value")
qty.observe(update, names="value")
qty.observe(remember, names="value")
update()
ui = widgets.VBox([price, qty, total])     # display(ui) in a notebook

qty.value = 5                              # as if the user moved the slider
print(total.value)                         # Total: 50.00
print(log)                                 # [(3, 5)]
takeaways: `interact` builds controls from a function's parameters in one line
Widgets have a `value`; react with `observe(..., names='value')` or `on_click`
Send callback output to a `widgets.Output()` area
pitfalls: Printing from a widget callback without an Output area, so the text ends up in JupyterLab's log instead of under the widget.

quiz.explain: interact turns a (min, max) tuple of whole numbers into an IntSlider.

concepts.name: Working effectively in JupyterLab
concepts.summary: Use JupyterLab's file browser, split views, consoles, terminals, debugger, table of contents and extensions.
concepts.why: JupyterLab is a full workspace; using it only to view one notebook leaves most of its usefulness on the table.
concepts.body:
JupyterLab shows documents and tools in tabs that you can drag to split the main area: for example a notebook beside the CSV file it reads, or two views of the same notebook.

Features worth knowing:

- **File browser** (left sidebar): opens notebooks, CSV files (shown as a grid), images, Markdown with a live preview, and a text editor that colours code by its parts.
- **Consoles**: right-click a notebook and choose "New Console for Notebook" for a scratch area attached to the same kernel, ideal for quick checks without cluttering the notebook.
- **Terminals**: a full terminal in the browser, handy when JupyterLab runs on another computer.
- **Running panel**: lists open kernels and terminals, so you can shut down forgotten ones that hold memory.
- **Table of contents**: built from Markdown headings, for moving around long notebooks.
- **Debugger**: turn on the bug icon of a notebook, then click line numbers to set **breakpoints**, places where the code pauses. While paused you can look at variables and the chain of function calls that led there (current ipykernel versions support this).
- **Contextual help** (Ctrl+I) shows documentation for whatever is under the cursor.
- **Collapsible cells and outputs**, and "Render Side-by-Side" to show a long output next to its code.
- **Real-time collaboration**, several people editing at once, via the `jupyter-collaboration` extension.

**Extensions** add features: a Git panel (`jupyterlab-git`) for version control, smarter completion and warnings about suspicious code (`jupyterlab-lsp`), or tools that tidy code layout automatically. In JupyterLab 4 most install with `pip`, with no extra build step; `jupyter labextension list` shows what is installed.
concepts.code:
jupyter lab --version                 # 4.6.x
jupyter labextension list             # installed front-end extensions

# Common extensions are plain pip packages in JupyterLab 4
pip install jupyterlab-git            # Git panel
pip install jupyterlab-lsp python-lsp-server   # completion, hover, linting
pip install jupyter-collaboration     # real-time collaboration

# Settings live in JSON and can be versioned per user
ls ~/.jupyter/lab/user-settings/@jupyterlab/
takeaways: Split the main area to work on several documents side by side
Attach a console to a notebook's kernel for scratch work
Use the Running panel, debugger and table of contents; add extensions with pip
pitfalls: Leaving many kernels running in the background, each one holding its data in memory.

quiz.q: You want to try quick expressions against a notebook's variables without adding cells to it. What do you use?
options: A console attached to the notebook's kernel
quiz.explain: A console for the notebook shares its kernel, so it sees the same variables without editing the document.

concepts.name: Exporting and executing notebooks
concepts.summary: Convert notebooks to HTML, PDF or scripts with nbconvert, and run them without a person, with parameters, using papermill.
concepts.why: Notebooks become reports and scheduled jobs only when they can be run and exported without anyone clicking.
concepts.body:
**nbconvert** turns a notebook into other formats:

```bash
jupyter nbconvert --to html report.ipynb      # web page to share, keeps outputs
jupyter nbconvert --to script analysis.ipynb  # .py file of the code cells
jupyter nbconvert --to webpdf report.ipynb    # PDF, drawn by an invisible browser
```

`--execute` runs all cells top to bottom in a fresh kernel before converting. That both refreshes the outputs and proves the notebook works from scratch. Add `--ExecutePreprocessor.timeout=600` to allow slow cells up to 600 seconds, and `--no-input` to hide the code and show only results, a common way to publish reports for people who don't program. `--to notebook --inplace --execute` updates the notebook itself.

**papermill** adds **parameters**. Tag one cell `parameters` (cell toolbar > tags) and put default values in it, such as `region = "eu"`. Then

```bash
papermill report.ipynb out/report_us.ipynb -p region us -p year 2026
```

inserts a new cell after it with the given values, runs the whole notebook and saves the result, outputs included, as a new notebook. Failed cells are highlighted in that copy, which makes it an excellent record of the run. papermill can also be called from Python, `papermill.execute_notebook(...)`, which is how scheduling tools such as Airflow run notebooks every night.

Under both tools sits **nbclient**, the library that starts a kernel and runs the cells one by one. For jobs that run regularly and must not break, keep notebooks for exploring and reporting, and move reusable code into importable `.py` modules that the notebook calls.
concepts.code:
# report.ipynb has a cell tagged "parameters": region = "eu"; year = 2025
jupyter nbconvert --to html --execute --no-input report.ipynb
#   [NbConvertApp] Writing ... bytes to report.html

jupyter nbconvert --to script report.ipynb       # -> report.py

papermill report.ipynb out/report_us.ipynb -p region us -p year 2026
#   Executing notebook with kernel: python3
#   (out/report_us.ipynb gets an injected cell: region = "us", year = 2026)

python - <<'EOF'
import papermill as pm
pm.execute_notebook("report.ipynb", "out/report_jp.ipynb",
                    parameters={"region": "jp"})
EOF
takeaways: `jupyter nbconvert --to html|script|webpdf` exports; `--execute` reruns first
`--no-input` publishes results without code
papermill inserts parameters after a tagged cell and saves a run copy
pitfalls: Exporting a notebook without `--execute`, shipping old outputs that the current code would no longer produce.

quiz.q: How does papermill know where to inject `-p region us`?
options: It looks for a cell tagged 'parameters' and inserts a new cell after it
It edits every assignment to region
quiz.explain: papermill adds an injected-parameters cell right after the cell tagged parameters, overriding its defaults.

concepts.name: Reproducible notebooks and version control
concepts.summary: Avoid hidden state, pin environments, strip outputs, pair notebooks with scripts via Jupytext, and compare them with nbdime.
concepts.why: A notebook that only works on one person's computer, in one kernel session, is not a result anyone can trust.
concepts.body:
A result is reproducible when someone else can rerun it and get the same answer. In notebooks, problems come from three places: state, environment and files.

**State.** Running cells out of order and deleting cells leave variables the notebook no longer defines. Restart and Run All before sharing. Better still, let an automatic check run `jupyter nbconvert --execute` (or papermill) on every change, for example in your team's CI system, so broken notebooks are caught at once. Set random seeds explicitly so random numbers repeat.

**Environment.** Record the exact versions of the libraries you use (`requirements.txt`, `uv.lock`, `environment.yml`), and give each project its own kernel. Print key versions in the first cell when results matter. Avoid full paths into your own home folder such as `/Users/ana/data.csv`; use paths relative to the project folder.

**Files and Git.** Git, the usual version control tool, works best with short text files. A `.ipynb` file is JSON that also stores outputs, execution counts and other details, so comparing two versions is noisy and images bloat the history. Options:

- **nbstripout** adds a Git filter that removes outputs whenever you commit (`nbstripout --install`).
- **Jupytext** pairs each notebook with a plain-text script, for example in the `py:percent` format, where `# %%` marks each cell. You review and compare the `.py` file, and Jupytext keeps both in step when you save. Many teams commit only the text version.
- **nbdime** compares and merges notebooks cell by cell (`nbdiff`, `nbmerge`), and plugs into Git with `nbdime config-git --enable`.

Keep heavy logic in importable modules with tests, and let notebooks call them and explain the story. A notebook that is mostly calls to well-named functions is easy to rerun, review and trust.
concepts.code:
# Pair a notebook with a percent-format script and keep them in step
jupytext --set-formats ipynb,py:percent analysis.ipynb
jupytext --sync analysis.ipynb         # updates whichever is older
head -3 analysis.py
#   # ---
#   # jupyter:
#   #   jupytext:     (settings header, then cells marked with # %%)

# Strip outputs automatically on commit
pip install nbstripout && nbstripout --install

# Cell-by-cell comparisons and merges in git
nbdime config-git --enable
git diff analysis.ipynb                # now shows changes per cell

# Prove it runs from scratch (e.g. in an automatic check)
jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute analysis.ipynb --output /tmp/ci.ipynb
takeaways: Restart and Run All, and run notebooks automatically on every change to catch hidden state
Pin library versions, use relative paths and set random seeds
Use nbstripout, Jupytext and nbdime to make notebooks Git-friendly
pitfalls: Committing notebooks with large outputs, so every rerun produces a huge, unreadable change in Git.

options: A paired .py script with `# %%` cell markers, kept in step with the notebook
quiz.explain: Jupytext pairs the notebook with a text version that is easy to compare and review.

concepts.name: The rich display protocol
concepts.summary: Make your own objects show up nicely in notebooks with _repr_html_ and _repr_mimebundle_, and update outputs in place with display IDs.
concepts.why: Library authors and power users can give any object a table, chart or custom view in Jupyter with a single method.
concepts.body:
When a notebook shows an object, IPython asks the object for versions of itself in several formats. Each format is named by a **MIME type**, a standard label such as `text/html` or `image/png`. All versions travel together to the browser page as a **MIME bundle**, and JupyterLab shows the richest one it can. An object joins in by defining special methods:

- `_repr_html_()` returns HTML (pandas tables use this);
- `_repr_markdown_()`, `_repr_latex_()`, `_repr_svg_()`, `_repr_png_()`, `_repr_json_()`;
- `_repr_mimebundle_(include=None, exclude=None)` returns the whole dict of MIME type to data, for full control, including custom types such as `application/vnd.plotly.v1+json`. Use either it or the individual methods, not both, so the result doesn't depend on how IPython combines them.

`__repr__` always supplies the `text/plain` version, used in terminals and by viewers that understand nothing richer. The whole bundle is saved in the notebook, so the same output can appear as HTML in JupyterLab and as text in a terminal viewer.

Return `None` from a `_repr_*_` method to say "no such version for this object", for example when it is too large to draw.

A **display ID** lets you update an existing output instead of adding new ones:

```python
h = display("starting...", display_id=True)
h.update("50% done")
```

Every output with that display ID changes, which is perfect for progress messages or live results.

For classes you didn't write, register a function that produces their HTML: `get_ipython().display_formatter.formatters["text/html"].for_type(MyType, func)`.
concepts.code: from IPython import get_ipython # run this in a notebook kernel from IPython.display import display class Money: def __init__(self, amount, currency): self.amount, self.currency = amount, currency def __repr__(self): return f"Money({self.amount}, {self.currency!r})" def _repr_html_(self): color = "green" if self.amount >= 0 else "red" return f"{self.amount:,.2f} {self.currency}" def _repr_markdown_(self): return f"**{self.amount:,.2f} {self.currency}**" m = Money(-1234.5, "EUR") data, meta = get_ipython().display_formatter.format(m) print(sorted(data)) # ['text/html', 'text/markdown', 'text/plain'] print(data["text/plain"]) # Money(-1234.5, 'EUR') h = display("step 1 of 3", display_id=True) # in a notebook: one output h.update("step 3 of 3") # ...updated in place
takeaways: IPython collects a MIME bundle of versions; JupyterLab shows the richest
Define `_repr_html_` or `_repr_mimebundle_` to give objects a rich view
`display(..., display_id=True)` returns a handle whose `update()` changes output in place
pitfalls: Returning enormous HTML from `_repr_html_`, which slows the browser and bloats saved notebooks.

quiz.q: Your class defines both `__repr__` and `_repr_html_`. What does JupyterLab show?
options: An error: only one is allowed
The HTML version, with the text/plain version kept as a fallback
quiz.explain: All versions are sent; JupyterLab shows the richest it supports, which is HTML.

concepts.name: The .ipynb format and nbformat
concepts.summary: Read, create, check and run notebooks from code, using the nbformat file structure and nbclient.
concepts.why: Tools such as code checkers, report builders, graders and conversion scripts all work by changing notebook JSON.
concepts.code:
import nbformat
from nbformat.v4 import new_notebook, new_code_cell, new_markdown_cell
from nbclient import NotebookClient

nb = new_notebook()
nb.cells = [
    new_markdown_cell("# Generated report"),
    new_code_cell("x = 21\nx * 2"),
    new_code_cell("print('done')", metadata={"tags": ["remove-input"]}),
]
nbformat.validate(nb)                       # raises if the schema is violated
NotebookClient(nb, timeout=60, kernel_name="python3").execute()

out = nb.cells[1].outputs[0]
print(out.output_type, out.data["text/plain"])   # execute_result 42
print(nb.cells[2].outputs[0].text.strip())       # done
print(nb.nbformat, nb.nbformat_minor >= 5, len(nb.cells[1].id) > 0)  # 4 True True
nbformat.write(nb, "report.ipynb")
takeaways: A notebook is JSON: cells with source, metadata and outputs, plus notebook metadata
Outputs are stream, execute_result, display_data or error objects holding MIME bundles
Use nbformat to read, build and validate notebooks, and nbclient to run them
pitfalls: Editing notebook JSON by hand with text replacement and producing files that fail validation.

quiz.q: Where is a cell's chart image stored in a run .ipynb file?
options: As base64 text in the cell's outputs (a display_data MIME bundle)
Nowhere; it is redrawn when the file opens
quiz.explain: Rich outputs are saved inside the file as MIME bundles, with images written as base64 text, which is why files grow.

concepts.name: Kernel architecture and the messaging protocol
concepts.summary: See how Jupyter interfaces talk to kernels through ZeroMQ channels and the messaging protocol, and drive a kernel from Python with jupyter_client.
concepts.why: The protocol explains kernel behaviour (busy/idle, interrupts, output in the wrong place) and lets you build tools that run code in kernels.
takeaways: Kernels exchange JSON messages over ZeroMQ channels: shell, iopub, stdin, control, heartbeat
Outputs are linked to their request through `parent_header.msg_id`
`jupyter_client` starts kernels and sends requests from Python
pitfalls: Expecting outputs on the shell channel; results and printed text are announced on iopub.

quiz.q: On which channel does a client receive printed output and the busy/idle status of a kernel?
quiz.explain: iopub announces everything a request produces, such as printed text, displays, results and status, to all clients.

concepts.name: Server security and multi-user deployment
concepts.summary: Run Jupyter safely on remote machines with tokens, passwords, TLS and SSH tunnels, and serve teams with JupyterHub.
concepts.why: A Jupyter server runs any code it is sent as its user, so an exposed or badly configured server hands an attacker full control of that account.
concepts.body:
A running Jupyter Server will run any code it receives, with all the permissions of the user who started it. Treat access to it like a login to that computer.

**Access.** By default the server makes up a random token and only accepts connections from `localhost`, the same machine. Keep both defaults whenever you can. To use a password instead, run `jupyter server password`, which stores a scrambled (hashed) version in the config folder. Never run with an empty token where other machines can reach the server, and avoid `--allow-root` outside containers.

**Remote machines.** The safest pattern is to keep the server on localhost and reach it through an **SSH tunnel**:

```bash
ssh -L 8888:localhost:8888 user@gpu-box
```

SSH forwards port 8888 on your laptop through its encrypted connection to port 8888 on the remote machine, so you open `http://localhost:8888` locally. If the server must accept network connections directly (`--ip 0.0.0.0`), protect the traffic with **TLS**, the encryption behind https (`--certfile` and `--keyfile`, or a reverse proxy in front), plus a strong password or token.

**Configuration** lives in `jupyter_server_config.py` (create it with `jupyter server --generate-config`) and uses **traitlets** settings such as `c.ServerApp.ip`, `c.ServerApp.port`, `c.ServerApp.root_dir`, `c.IdentityProvider.token`. Every option also works on the command line, e.g. `--ServerApp.port=9000`. `jupyter --paths` shows where config, data and runtime files live.

**Teams.** **JupyterHub** logs users in (with company accounts, GitHub and others) and starts a separate Jupyter server for each person: on one machine, in Docker containers, or on a Kubernetes cluster (the "Zero to JupyterHub" guide). Limits on memory and CPU, shutting down idle servers and shared storage are all set up at the hub.

Remember that a notebook from someone else can contain harmful code or outputs. Jupyter treats such notebooks as untrusted and won't run their JavaScript outputs until you mark them trusted.
concepts.code:
# Remote GPU box: keep the server on localhost and tunnel to it
ssh -L 8888:localhost:8888 me@gpu-box
jupyter lab --no-browser --port 8888       # run on gpu-box (listens on localhost)

# Set a password instead of copying tokens around
jupyter server password                    # stores a hashed password

# Generate and edit the config file
jupyter server --generate-config           # ~/.jupyter/jupyter_server_config.py
cat >> ~/.jupyter/jupyter_server_config.py <<'EOF'
c.ServerApp.ip = "127.0.0.1"
c.ServerApp.root_dir = "/srv/projects"
c.ServerApp.open_browser = False
EOF

jupyter --paths                            # config, data and runtime locations
# Teams: JupyterHub spawns one server per user (pip install jupyterhub)
takeaways: A Jupyter server runs any code it's sent as its user: protect it like a login
Keep localhost and tokens; use SSH tunnels, or TLS plus passwords, for remote access
Configure with traitlets (`c.ServerApp...`); use JupyterHub for teams
pitfalls: Starting `jupyter lab --ip 0.0.0.0` with an empty token on a rented cloud machine, handing control of it to anyone on the internet.

quiz.q: You need to use Jupyter on a remote server from your laptop. What is the safest common setup?
options: Run with --ip 0.0.0.0 and no token for convenience
Turn off logging in and rely on an unusual port
Keep the server on localhost and connect through an SSH tunnel
quiz.explain: An SSH tunnel keeps the server unreachable from the network while you reach it over an encrypted connection.
